turns.prompt_text: I own 2 6" fluorescent lights and a 12" uv fluorescent light, what are my options for ballasts?
turns.response_html:
Finding ballasts for smaller fluorescent lamps like your 6" and 12" tubes can be a bit of a scavenger hunt because modern lighting has shifted heavily toward LED. However, you still have a few solid paths depending on whether you want to stick with traditional tech or modernize the fixtures.

First, you need to identify your bulbs by their F-number, which is usually printed on the glass near the end:

  • 6-inch bulb: Usually an F4T5 (4 Watts).
  • 12-inch bulb (UV): Usually an F8T5 (8 Watts).

Here are your options for powering them:

1. Dedicated Linear Fluorescent Ballasts

You need a ballast specifically rated for low-wattage T5 lamps. Most standard "shop light" ballasts are for 32W or 54W lamps and will instantly burn out your small tubes.

  • Electronic Ballasts: Look for "T5 Electronic Ballasts" rated for 4W to 13W. Brands like Antron, Robertson, or IOTA often make multi-lamp ballasts that can run two F4T5s or a single F8T5.
  • Magnetic Ballasts: These are the "old school" heavy bricks. They are harder to find now but are incredibly durable. You would specifically search for a "Preheat Ballast" for 4W/8W lamps. These require a separate starter (usually an S2 or FS-5) to preheat the filaments before the lamp strikes.

2. Battery-Powered or DC Inverter Ballasts

Since these are small, low-wattage lamps, they are often used in portable lanterns or emergency lights.

  • If you are building a DIY project (like a portable UV mineral light), you can buy 6V or 12V DC Inverter Ballasts. These allow you to run your fluorescent tubes off a battery pack or a wall adapter without needing a massive high-voltage transformer.

3. The "Donor" Strategy (The Most Cost-Effective)

Buying a brand-new, high-quality ballast for a single 6" tube can sometimes cost more than a whole new fixture.

  • Under-cabinet fixtures: You can often find cheap, basic under-cabinet fluorescent fixtures at hardware stores or thrift shops. You can harvest the internal ballast from these to use in your specific setup. Just ensure the wattage on the "donor" fixture matches your 4W or 8W bulbs.

Important Considerations

  • UV Safety: Since your 12" bulb is UV, ensure the ballast provides a steady current. Flickering can sometimes shorten the life of the specialized phosphors in UV lamps. Always wear eye protection when testing UV tubes.
  • Total Wattage: If you plan to run both 6" bulbs off one ballast, ensure the ballast is rated for "2 x F4T5." If you "series" them on a single-lamp ballast, they likely won't strike (turn on) because the voltage drop is too high.

Would you like me to help you find a specific wiring diagram for a multi-lamp setup, or are you looking for a recommendation on a specific brand available near Ames?

turns.prompt_text: where can I go to find one
turns.response_html:
Finding ballasts for T5 tubes in these specific lengths (6" and 12") can be a bit tricky at standard big-box stores, as they primarily stock ballasts for larger 4-foot shop lights.

Since you are in the Ames area, here are your best local and specialty options:

1. Electrical Supply Houses (Best for Specialized Parts)

For small wattage ballasts (4W and 8W), a dedicated electrical distributor is much more likely to have the exact T5 electronic ballast you need than a general hardware store.

  • Echo Electric Supply: Located at 314 S 17th St, Ames. They specialize in professional-grade electrical components and can often order specific ballasts if they aren't on the shelf.
  • Van Meter Inc. (Ames): Another professional supplier that handles industrial and commercial lighting components.

2. Local Hardware Stores

Standard retailers in town often carry "universal" ballasts, but you must check the label to ensure they support F4T5 or F8T5 bulbs.

  • Lowe’s Home Improvement (Ames): Located at 120 Airport Rd. They have a "Commercial Lighting" section where they stock ballasts from brands like GE and Philips. Look for T5-specific models.
  • Menards (Ames): Located at 700 S Duff Ave. Menards typically has a large "Ballasts & Starters" section near the light bulbs. They are a good place to look for the "Preheat" style ballasts if you are working with an older fixture.
  • O'Donnell Ace Hardware: Located at 615 24th St. While their selection is smaller, they are excellent for finding small parts and might carry the individual starters needed for magnetic ballasts.

3. Specialty UV & Hobby Shops

Because your 12" UV light is often used in specific hobbies, you might find ballasts at shops that don't specialize in general home lighting:

  • Pet/Aquarium Stores: Small UV lights are common in reptile enclosures and aquarium sterilizers. Stores like Petco or local specialty fish shops in the area sometimes carry replacement ballasts for these small fixtures.
  • Hydroponic Stores: UV lighting is frequently used in indoor gardening.

Pro-Tip for Ames Residents

If you strike out at the major retailers, check the Habitat for Humanity ReStore on South Bell Ave. They often have older, small under-cabinet fixtures for a few dollars. You can "harvest" the ballast from one of those fixtures to use for your specific bulbs.

Before you go: Check the wattage on your bulbs. Most 6" tubes are 4 Watts and 12" tubes are 8 Watts. If you call Echo Electric or Ace, ask specifically for a "T5 ballast for a 4-watt or 8-watt lamp."

turns.prompt_text: I feel like if I go into a pet store like more of a boutique store they're going to upcharge me where could I go with it being electronics store or hardware store I should go to
turns.response_html:
To avoid the "boutique" pricing of pet stores while staying away from the limited stock of big-box retailers, your best bet in Ames is to go where the professional contractors and local engineers go.

Since you're a software engineer with an interest in DIY and electronics, you’ll likely find these spots more useful for your project than a general hardware store:

1. Echo Electric Supply (314 S 17th St, Ames)

This is a professional electrical distributor. Unlike a pet store or a high-end lighting boutique, they sell parts based on industrial catalogs.

  • Why go here: They deal in the actual components. If you walk in and ask for a "T5 ballast for 4-watt and 8-watt lamps," they will look through their commercial inventory. Even if it’s not on the shelf, they can usually get it from their warehouse in a day or two at a fair "contractor" price.
  • Pro Tip: They are open 7:00 AM – 5:00 PM Monday through Friday but closed on weekends.

2. O'Donnell Ace Hardware (615 24th St, Ames)

While it is a hardware store, Ace locations are independently owned and often carry a much deeper "bits and bobs" inventory than Lowe’s or Menards.

  • Why go here: They are known for having those specific, hard-to-find electrical parts like starters and small-wattage ballasts tucked away in the back aisles. It’s the kind of place where you can find individual components rather than having to buy a whole new fixture.

3. Interstate All Battery Center (220 Airport Rd, Ames)

Because you are working with very small 6" and 12" tubes, these are often used in portable or emergency lighting that runs on DC power (batteries).

  • Why go here: If you’re planning to build a custom enclosure or something portable, they have expertise in the small inverters and battery-side electronics that power these specific types of bulbs. They are right across from Lowe's, making it an easy double-stop.

4. ISU Surplus (Ames/Campus)

Given your background and location, check the Iowa State University Surplus sales.

  • Why go here: They frequently retire lab equipment, old under-cabinet lighting from dorm renovations, and specialized electronics. You can often find entire crates of older lighting fixtures or "parts" units for almost nothing. It’s a great way to "harvest" a ballast for a few dollars.

What to ask for to avoid the "Retail Markup":

When you walk in, avoid saying you need it for a "pet light" or "UV light." Simply provide the technical specs:

  • "I'm looking for an electronic ballast for F4T5 and F8T5 fluorescent lamps."
  • If they ask for the application, just say it's for an under-cabinet fixture or a DIY electronics project. This keeps the conversation focused on the standard electrical part rather than a "specialty" hobby item.
